title: Hidden Costs in Library Calls (C# and Python)
oneLiner: One line of library code can be a whole loop: slicing, in on a list, insert at the front, LINQ, string +=, max() in a loop.
keyTakeaway: Before you multiply, price every call inside the loop. Anything that copies (slices, Substring, ToList, path + [x]), scans (Contains or in on a list, count, max, LINQ with a predicate) or shifts (insert or remove at the front) is O(n), and an O(n) call inside an O(n) loop is O(n²) no matter how short the line looks.
explanation:
The cost per trip in Step 2 of the analysis procedure is where most wrong answers come from, because library calls hide their loops. A Python slice a[1:] or a C# range a[1..] on an array copies the rest of it. x in my_list and List.Contains walk the list. list.pop(0) and RemoveAt(0) shift every remaining element. max(a), sum(a) and LINQ's Count(predicate) all scan. None of these look like loops, and each one is O(n).

Strings deserve extra care. They are immutable in both C# and Python, so building one with += in a loop copies everything built so far on every trip: O(n²) in the total length. CPython sometimes avoids the copy when nothing else refers to the string, but that is an optimization you cannot rely on, so write "".join(parts) in Python and use StringBuilder (or string.Join, string.Concat) in C#. Comparing or hashing a string is O(L) in its length, which is why a dictionary keyed by words is O(L) per operation, not O(1).

LINQ and generators are lazy. Chaining Where and Select is still one pass when you finally enumerate it, which is good. The trap is the opposite: enumerating the same lazy query more than once (calling Count(), then ElementAt, then foreach) reruns the whole pipeline every time. Materialize it once with ToList() if you need it again.

Sorting is O(n log n) in time in both languages, but the extra space differs: Array.Sort and List.Sort in C# are introsort with O(log n) recursion, LINQ OrderBy buffers O(n) and is stable, and Python's Timsort can use O(n) extra. Say which one you are using when you state space.

For each trap below, look at the C# and Python versions, predict the total, then reveal the reason and the fix. The table under it is a reference for the calls that show up in interview code most.
